clue.text: He put a loge in the theatre, added helmsman for successful farce

definitions.text: He put a loge in the theatre, added helmsman for successful farce

parts.words: He put a loge in the theatre, added helmsman for successful farce
parts.note: a loge is a theatre box and a helmsman is a cox, so the clue describes the playwright of the Victorian farce Box and Cox

explanation.surface: A theatre impresario installs a private box and hires a boatman, and the show is a hit.
explanation.walkthrough: Box and Cox (1847) was a hugely successful one-act farce; a loge is a box and a rowing helmsman a cox.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian dramatist wrote the farce Box and Cox, whose title the box and the helmsman spell out.

clue.text: Reginald Rose's was very cross

parts.note: Reginald Rose wrote Twelve Angry Men, the play about a body of twelve deliberating citizens, so his was 'very cross'

explanation.surface: Someone recalls that the writer Reginald Rose was in a furious temper.
explanation.walkthrough: Rose's play and film Twelve Angry Men is set entirely in a deliberation room; the twelve angry men form the panel.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve Angry Men depicts a trial panel of citizens, all of them angry, hence 'very cross'.

clue.text: A stack, say, of humility

definitions.note: the 'umble clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield, a byword for false humility

indicators.note: say signals that the word for a stack is to be spoken and its sound kept

explanation.surface: A pile of something, supposedly made of modesty.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah, the fawning clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield, is forever 'ever so 'umble'.
explanation.definitionFit: Uriah, the Dickens villain, constantly professes his lowliness, making him the character of humility.

clue.text: Old hat stuff from William Plomer?

definitions.meaning: the title of a 1952 novel by the South African-born writer William Plomer

explanation.surface: Something out of date, perhaps by a twentieth-century novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Outdated things are relics fit for display in a gallery of antiquities, and Plomer's novel bears the same title.

clue.text: Ignited once more in extempore literature ()

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the run of the words extempore literature

explanation.surface: Something set alight again within improvised writing.
explanation.definitionFit: To be set on fire a second time is to be kindled again.

clue.text: More gin is stirred (or shaken), revealing a view on Christian theology

indicators.note: a drink that is stirred has its contents mixed, so these letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A cocktail joke about Bond's martini preference leads into theology.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stirred (or shaken)' plays on the martini order; 'stirred' rearranges MORE GIN IS.
explanation.definitionFit: The teachings of the third-century theologian Origen of Alexandria form a doctrinal school.

clue.text: Main adaptation of Patrick Leigh Fermor

indicators.note: an adaptation reworks its source, so the letters of main are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A principal film version of a travel writer's book.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a metonym: the travel writer stands for his 1958 book about the southern Peloponnese.
explanation.definitionFit: Leigh Fermor's travel book about the Peloponnese peninsula has this title.

clue.text: Confused a claim about Kentish rebel in theory

indicators.note: about means the mixed letters go around the rebel
confused means jumbled, so the letters of a claim are mixed up

parts.note: Jack Cade led the 1450 Kentish rebellion

explanation.surface: A muddled assertion about a fifteenth-century insurgent, put forward speculatively.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Cade led the 1450 rising in Kent, made famous in Shakespeare's Henry VI Part 2. 'Confused' scrambles the two words, and 'about' wraps them round him.
explanation.definitionFit: Something scholarly and theoretical rather than practical exists only as an idea.

clue.text: "Resolved to be ——, adamant for drift" (Churchill)

parts.note: a fill-in from Churchill's 1936 attack on Baldwin's government, decided only to be undecided

explanation.surface: A quotation from Churchill mocking a government's paralysis.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line: 'decided only to be undecided, resolved to be ..., adamant for drift'; each phrase is a paradox.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means wavering or indecisive, the paradox Churchill pinned on the cabinet.

clue.text: Virgin mother of Roman fathers

parts.note: the Vestal priestess who bore Romulus and Remus, founders of Rome

explanation.surface: A paradoxical virgin who mothered the founders of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend the Vestal priestess was made pregnant by Mars and bore the twin founders of the city.

clue.text: A vehicle, say, for A Month in the Country author

definitions.text: A Month in the Country author

indicators.note: say signals that the word for a vehicle is spoken and its sound kept

explanation.surface: Something to drive, perhaps, for a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: J. L. Carr wrote the 1980 novel A Month in the Country.
explanation.definitionFit: The English novelist J. L. Carr wrote that Booker-shortlisted book.

clue.text: "Ding dong, Bell, Pussy's in the well" is a measure of it, Hopkins said

definitions.text: "Ding dong, Bell, Pussy's in the well" is a measure of it, Hopkins said

parts.words: "Ding dong, Bell, Pussy's in the well" is a measure of it, Hopkins said
parts.note: Gerard Manley Hopkins cited the nursery rhyme as an example of his stress-based metre

explanation.surface: A Victorian poet's remark about a nursery rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: Hopkins pointed to nursery rhymes like 'Ding dong bell' as instances of the metre he named.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopkins coined the term for verse measured by stresses, not syllables, and cited the rhyme as a model.

clue.text: Ludwig Bemelmans work exerts quip so inefficiently

indicators.note: done inefficiently, the letters fall out of order and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A remark about a clumsy joke made by straining.
explanation.walkthrough: Bemelmans, author of Madeline, wrote a 1966 book named after an Ecuadorean train.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian-American writer published a travel book with this title about an Ecuadorean railway.

clue.text: Calling of Shavian Galatea

parts.note: Shaw's Pygmalion recasts the Galatea myth; Eliza Doolittle sells blooms at Covent Garden

explanation.surface: The vocation of a statue brought to life in Shaw's version.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calling' looks like a cry but means occupation; Eliza Doolittle is Shaw's Galatea.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliza Doolittle earns her living selling blooms on London streets, her trade at the play's start.

clue.text: Troublesome rats rid via instrument maker

indicators.note: troublesome rats run amok, signalling the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Pests eliminated by way of a craftsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio of Cremona was the most famous violin builder.

clue.text: Odyssey's acquiescent exiles hop gaol, it is absurd

indicators.note: absurd suggests nonsense, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Homeric characters escape prison in ridiculous fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Odyssey the lotus-eaters live in drugged contentment, forgetting home.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's lotus-eaters were content to stay idle, having eaten the narcotic fruit.

clue.text: A friend of Isaac, with philistine outlook

definitions.text: A friend of Isaac, with philistine outlook

parts.words: A friend of Isaac, with philistine outlook
parts.note: the Philistine king of Gerar made a covenant with Isaac in Genesis

explanation.surface: An uncultured companion of a patriarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Philistine' means uncultured in the surface, but the king of Gerar was literally Philistine.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical king of Gerar swore a pact of peace with Isaac, a Philistine ruler.

clue.text: Powerful angel decapitates Miss Spark

indicators.note: decapitates means the head, the first letter, is cut off

explanation.surface: A mighty heavenly being beheads a novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the archangels, named in Milton's Paradise Lost as regent of the sun.

clue.text: Shape of cloud, as Polonius agreed ()

definitions.text: Shape of cloud, as Polonius agreed

parts.words: Shape of cloud, as Polonius agreed
parts.note: in Hamlet Polonius humours the prince over a cloud's shape, ending with 'Very like a...'

explanation.surface: A Hamlet courtier assents about a form in the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet teases Polonius: the cloud is a camel, a weasel, and finally a sea mammal.
explanation.definitionFit: Polonius agrees the cloud is 'very like' the great sea mammal Hamlet names last.

clue.text: Fast protagonist

parts.note: Howard Fast wrote the novel The ..., about newcomers to America

explanation.surface: A speedy hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like speedy but is the American novelist Howard Fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast's saga follows a newcomer who arrives in America to settle there.

clue.text: Chunkier fees renegotiated for Goethe's poem (75)

indicators.note: terms renegotiated are rearranged, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Larger payments agreed afresh for a German classic.
explanation.definitionFit: Goethe's 1794 mock epic retells the beast fable of the fox Reynard.

clue.text: Reminiscent of a disastrous performance of The Apple Cart? ()

definitions.text: Reminiscent of a disastrous performance of The Apple Cart?

parts.words: Reminiscent of a disastrous performance of The Apple Cart?
parts.note: The Apple Cart is a Shaw play; spoiling plans is to overturn the apple cart

explanation.surface: Recalling a botched staging of Shaw's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'upset the apple cart' means to spoil arrangements; Shaw's play gives the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Overturned, as in the idiom about spoiling plans.

clue.text: Liberated as Golding's Fall

definitions.meaning: William Golding's 1959 novel is titled ___ Fall

explanation.surface: Released, like a novel by William Golding.
explanation.definitionFit: Released means at liberty, and Golding's novel title completes with the same word.

clue.text: "As it, it ain't. That's logic." (Carroll)

parts.note: Tweedledee's contrariwise argument in Through the Looking-Glass has a gap to fill

explanation.surface: A quotation of Tweedledee's nonsense reasoning.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line: 'but as it ..., it ain't. That's logic.'
explanation.definitionFit: Tweedledee's contraction for 'is not' completes the line.

clue.text: Companion to Cleopatra in fair assessment

indicators.note: in tells us the answer lies within the words fair assessment

explanation.surface: An attendant to a queen getting an honest appraisal.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Egyptian queen has two waiting-women, Charmian and this one.

clue.text: Novel form of sutra I used for pitch levels

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Novel form of sutra I used for pitch levels': SUTRA I USED has U, D where TESSITURAS needs T, S (likely 'sutra I sets'); too many letters off for an OCR or slip correction and no source found
annotationWithheld.clue: Novel form of sutra I used for pitch levels

clue.text: Secular leaders of lost allegory in Comus

indicators.note: leaders are the front runners, so the first letter of each word is taken

explanation.surface: Worldly ideas at the head of Milton's masque.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay and non-clerical, as opposed to belonging to the clergy.

clue.text: The part-time typist estimated by Shakespeare

parts.note: a temp is a temporary office worker
est. is the abbreviation for estimated

explanation.surface: A temporary secretary's guess at a playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's late romance, set on Prospero's island, was written by him.
